entry.content:
Publish the release from a draft with every file attached, and let GitHub cut the tag

The first attempt pushed the tag by hand, then handed gh the artifact folders themselves - the
download keeps each glob's folder - and failed on the first one, leaving a tag with no release,
which the next run would have read as done. Now the files are listed one by one, the release is
created as a draft and published in one step, GitHub creates the tag at that moment, and a draft
left by a run that died is removed by the next run's version check.

entry.title: Open the window on a starting page in the page's own colour, and read…
entry.content:
Open the window on a starting page in the page's own colour, and read the original in the same ink as the translation

The window used to be created only once the server answered, which left a second or two with
no window at all and then a white webview while the real page loaded. It now opens at once on a
bundled starting page, painted behind with the client's own background for the system theme, and
is navigated to the server when /api/health answers; the server is started off the UI thread.
In the reader the source column was a step lighter than the translation and read as dim rather
than recessed.

entry.title: Reposition the macOS traffic lights for the taller merged bar
entry.content:
Reposition the macOS traffic lights for the taller merged bar

The overlay title bar's traffic-light centring assumed the 38px bar
the first cut of the window chrome used. Now that every screen's own
48px bar is the window's title bar on every platform, the lights
would sit near the top edge instead of centred. traffic_light_position
puts them back at Apple's own left margin, centred in the new height.

Also rewrites the desktop README's "Window chrome" section for the
merged design: no separate WindowChrome.vue, one bar height on every
platform, and the caption buttons pressed flush against the window's
own right and top edges on Windows (Linux's round buttons keep a
6px exception on their trailing edge so the corner radius is not
clipped).

entry.title: Merge the window chrome into every screen's own header bar
entry.content:
Merge the window chrome into every screen's own header bar

Each screen already had exactly one 48px <header class="bar"> at the
top. Inside the desktop shell, WindowChrome.vue stacked a second,
separate 32px bar above it with its own wordmark - the same word
twice, one atop the other. That component goes away; its job (the
drag region, the three caption buttons, the macOS traffic-light
inset) moves into the screens' own header, which becomes the
window's title bar when running in the shell and looks byte-for-byte
identical to what it always was in a browser.

- AppBar.vue: the shared header every screen now renders instead of
  its own <header class="bar">. Carries data-tauri-drag-region on
  itself and its internal slot wrapper when in the shell, so a
  mousedown anywhere non-interactive falls through to start a window
  drag; screens mark that content with a data-bar-text attribute
  rather than the component walking their DOM. Draws the macOS
  traffic-light inset and renders WindowControls after the slot.
- WindowControls.vue: the three caption buttons, drawn with the
  platform's own glyphs - Segoe Fluent Icons on Windows, the app's
  Material Symbols icons in round GNOME-style buttons on Linux,
  nothing on macOS. Replaces the first cut's hand-drawn SVG lines.
- shell.ts: chromeLayoutFor is gone along with the per-platform bar
  height it computed - the bar is 48px everywhere now. parseDesktopShell
  and useDesktopShell are unchanged.
- The ten screens (library, novel, reader, alignment, settings,
  novel settings, parsers, and the three import screens) swap their
  own <header class="bar"> for <AppBar>, content unchanged, and mark
  their non-interactive bar text with data-bar-text. The reader keeps
  its own hide-on-scroll bar by passing a class through to AppBar's
  root and overriding it with :deep().
- DefaultLayout.vue no longer renders a separate chrome bar.

Verified byte-for-byte identical bar geometry against a build of
main in a headless browser (library, novel, reader, settings,
parsers): same height, same first/last content element positions,
in both states.

entry.title: Draw the client's own window chrome inside the shell
entry.content:
Draw the client's own window chrome inside the shell

WindowChrome.vue renders above .content in DefaultLayout.vue, but only
when window.__NEKTO_DESKTOP__ says this page is running inside the
shell - nothing changes in a browser tab, not one pixel. Bar height,
control side and shape come from the platform: 32px with square
caption buttons on Windows, 40px with round ones on Linux, 38px with
no buttons of our own on macOS, which reserves a 78px inset for the
real traffic lights instead. Double-click toggles maximize through
Tauri's own drag-region handling; nothing here listens for it by hand.

src/desktop/shell.ts is the client's half of the contract: it parses
the global once, defensively, and exposes isMaximized / isFullscreen
kept current from the Tauri window API and the nekto:fullscreen event,
plus the three button actions. It reaches window.__TAURI__ directly,
typed by hand, rather than adding @tauri-apps/api as a dependency of
what is otherwise an ordinary web app. The pure parts - parsing the
global and choosing a platform's bar height and control side - get
their own vitest spec.

entry.title: Make the desktop window frameless and tell the page which platform it…
entry.content:
Make the desktop window frameless and tell the page which platform it is on

Windows and Linux drop native decorations outright; macOS keeps the real
traffic lights via an overlay title bar with the title hidden. Windows
also gets the DWM shadow back explicitly, and Linux gets an 8px
edge/corner resize script since an undecorated window there loses its
resize border entirely (Windows keeps native resize on an undecorated
window, so it needs nothing extra).

tauri-plugin-window-state is told to stop restoring the decorated flag
it saves per window - left alone, it silently re-decorated a window
this crate had just built frameless, using whatever was saved to disk
on an earlier run.

An initialization script writes window.__NEKTO_DESKTOP__ = { platform,
version } before the page's own scripts run, on every navigation - the
whole contract the client's own window chrome reads. The fullscreen
script also now dispatches a nekto:fullscreen DOM event on toggle, so
the client can hide its bar without polling isFullscreen().

The capability file grants exactly what the bar's own code calls:
dragging and its double-click maximize, the three caption actions, the
state the buttons render, and the Linux resize script - each checked
against the generated capabilities schema.

entry.title: Cut releases from main instead of a hand-pushed tag
entry.content:
Cut releases from main instead of a hand-pushed tag

.github/workflows/release.yml watches main. version reads
Directory.Build.props and checks whether that version is already tagged and
released; build only runs for a new version, and builds Windows and Linux
desktop installers plus a standalone server zip for each; release only runs
once every build has succeeded, and tags the commit, creates the GitHub
release, and writes a changelog from the commit history since the previous
tag. A build failure leaves no tag and no release, so the next push retries.
The old desktop-release.yml, triggered by a hand-pushed tag, is folded into
this and removed.

The three jobs never cancel a run in progress (concurrency group with
cancel-in-progress: false), since a release that is half-uploaded must
finish rather than be cut off by the next push.

entry.content:
License the repository GPL-3.0-or-later

The vendored WebToEpub parsers under NektoTranslate.Server/vendor/WebToEpub
are GPL-3.0, and shipping them inside this application places the whole
distributed work under the same terms. LICENSE carries the verbatim GPL-3.0

entry.title: Read the desktop build's version from Directory.Build.props
entry.content:
Read the desktop build's version from Directory.Build.props

Directory.Build.props stays the single source of the application's version.
scripts/publish-server.mjs now defaults -p:Version to whatever it holds
instead of requiring NEKTO_BUILD_VERSION, so a plain local build stamps the
same version CI would. A new scripts/sync-version.mjs writes that same value
into tauri.conf.json, Cargo.toml and package.json, and npm run build runs it
first; --check compares instead of writing, for CI to catch drift. Along the
way, Directory.Build.props and package.json also pick up the GPL-3.0-or-later
license metadata the vendored WebToEpub parsers require of the whole build.
